newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Former Irish minister denies trying to evade tax.
newsitem.headline: Former Irish minister denies trying to evade tax.

text.p: Former Irish transport minister Michael Lowry said on Thursday that money paid by leading Irish department chain Dunnes Stores for the renovation of his home was income earned for professional services and denied he was attempting to evade tax.

Lowry, who was a rising star within the Fine Gael party, resigned abruptly in November after admitting a newspaper report that Dunnes paid for the extension and renovation of his private home in County Tipperary in 1992.
He was chairman of the party's parliamentary group at the time and head of his own company, Streamline Enterprises, which provided refrigeration systems for Dunnes Stores throughout Ireland.
In a special statement to parliament on Thursday, he said that any money spent on his house was income payable to him in respect of nothing other than professional refrigeration advice and service.

"This had nothing whatsoever to do with my role as a TD (member of parliament) or subsequently as a minister...It was not a loan. It was not a gift. It was not a handout. It was income", he said, adding that the renovation "was not designed by me as a tax evasion measure".
Lowry said he had not told Ireland's Revenue Commissioners about the payment because he was disputing the value of the work done.

"The truth is that the total value of this work has not been determined to my satisfaction," he said in a 45-minute address to parliament. Lowry said Dunnes Stores claims to have spent 395,000 punts on the renovation, a figure he rejects.

But the former minister admitted he had availed of a 1993 Irish tax amnesty and said that some of his tax obligations were still outstanding. He also said he had not received proper planning permission for the extension but said this was now in train.
"As a minister and as a politician I discharged my responsibilities properly," Lowry said.

"As a businessman I left unfinished commercial business behind me. In my business life, I accept that I have been culpable in that I did not fully deal with the responsibilities arising from my business affairs in a timely fashion."
Explaining why he had resigned, Lowry said that procrastination would have damaged the three-party coalition government.
"I felt it would not have been possible while I was a minister to explain what I genuinely believe to be a proper and legitimate transaction but nevertheless a complex one," he said.
But he said he was staying on as a member of parliament and promised to run for election again.

The Dunnes payments to Lowry came to light in a report by a firm of chartered accountants which also showed that the privately-owned department store, which has clothing and food outlets in every major Irish town and city, had made several similar payments.
The report has been given to a retired judge who will examine it and extract the names of politicians and public officials who received money from Dunnes.
The names will then be given to parliament's committee on procedures and privileges which will decide whether anyone has a case to answer.
